newsitem.title: USA: Round-the-world balloonist heads for Atlantic.
newsitem.headline: Round-the-world balloonist heads for Atlantic.

text.p: American Steve Fossett, hours into his attempt to become the first person to circle the globe in a balloon, gave the go-ahead on Tuesday to start the Atlantic Ocean leg of his 18-day journey.
The 52-year-old Colorado commodities broker was between Lexington, Kentucky, and Knoxville, Tennessee, at daybreak after lifting off from St. Louis late on Monday night.
"Things are going very well," said Bo Kemper, spokesman for the Chicago-based expedition.

"He's moving at about 50 miles per hour (80 kph). About a half hour ago he committed to go across the Atlantic, which is a very big step" -- and one the expedition considered a crucial point of no return.

Kemper said one heater in the balloon's gondola was not working but a backup unit was functioning in the sub-zero cold. Fossett planned to head over the Atlantic somewhere along the coast of North Carolina.

His exact route will depend on wind currents, although he has clearance to pass over several dozen countries. He was to maintain an altitude of from 18,000 to 24,000 feet (5,500 to 7,300 metres) -- lower than two rival missions that failed within the past week to crack one of manned flight's most difficult barriers.

Fossett, who made a fortune in the Chicago futures markets before taking to a life of record-seeking adventures in the air and on water, lifted off on his solo flight late on Monday night from Busch Stadium in downtown St. Louis, drifting over the Mississippi River and across Illinois.
A similar attempt by Fossett one year ago, launched from South Dakota, ended in failure when his shredded balloon crashed on a frozen lake in Canada.

On Sunday, a balloon piloted by Bertrand Piccard and Wim Verstraeten ditched in the Mediterranean six hours after taking off from the Swiss Alps. Fumes from kerosene leaking into the cabin brought down the Swiss-Belgian team.

Last Wednesday British tycoon Richard Branson and two crew members brought their Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria less than 24 hours after taking off from Morocco. The craft had suddenly lost lift and plunged.
Unlike the other recent expeditions, Fossett is flying alone. He already holds a world distance record for a solo balloon flight set in 1995 when he flew from South Korea to Canada.
His "Solo Spirit" craft gets its lift from helium and hot air, as did the Swiss-Belgian and British craft.
Jet streams dipping farther south at high speeds during the Northern Hemisphere winter make January a favoured time for such long-distance balloon flights.
